source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Structural induction on formulas
statement: If a property holds for sentence symbols and is preserved by each connective formation rule, it holds for every well-formed formula.
conditions: The property is defined for all formulas.
conclusion: The property holds for all formulas generated by the grammar.
typical_uses: Prove unique readability and semantic recursion facts.
common_misuses: Inducting on string length without handling subformula structure.
bridge_lemmas: Every compound formula has immediate subformulas of smaller construction depth.
repair_templates: Use the formation rule as the induction step.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Recursive truth evaluation
statement: A truth assignment extends uniquely from sentence symbols to all formulas by evaluating connectives according to their truth tables.
conditions: A valuation assigns T or F to each sentence symbol.
conclusion: Every formula has a unique truth value under the valuation.
typical_uses: Define satisfaction and prove semantic equivalences.
common_misuses: Leaving the value of compound formulas unspecified.
repair_templates: Evaluate formulas bottom-up from their immediate subformulas.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Sentential compactness theorem
statement: If every finite subset of a set of sentential formulas is satisfiable, then the whole set is satisfiable.
conditions: The formulas use a common set of sentence symbols.
typical_uses: Build models from consistent finite fragments.
common_misuses: Confusing finite validity with finite satisfiability.
bridge_lemmas: Truth assignments form a product of two-point spaces.
repair_templates: Check every finite subset, then invoke compactness.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Truth in a structure
statement: A structure interprets function and relation symbols over a nonempty domain; term values and formula truth are defined recursively under variable assignments.
conditions: A first-order language and a structure for it are fixed.
conclusion: Each term has a value and each formula has a definite truth value under an assignment.
common_misuses: Ignoring free-variable assignments or symbol arities.
bridge_lemmas: Substitution lemma for terms and formulas.
repair_templates: State the domain, interpretations, and assignment explicitly.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Substitution lemma
statement: The value of a term after substituting terms for variables equals the value obtained by evaluating the substituted terms first; the analogous formula statement preserves satisfaction under assignment update.
conditions: Substitution is capture-avoiding and an interpretation is fixed.
conclusion: Syntactic substitution commutes with semantic evaluation.
typical_uses: Prove validity of quantified formulas and formalize replacement.
bridge_lemmas: Structural induction on terms and formulas.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Soundness and completeness
statement: For the first-order deductive calculus, every derivable sentence is logically valid, and every logically valid sentence is derivable.
conditions: The calculus and semantics are the standard first-order ones.
conclusion: Provability and validity coincide for sentences.
typical_uses: Convert semantic entailment into formal proofs and detect invalid derivations.
common_misuses: Applying completeness to theories with inconsistent premises without noting vacuity.
bridge_lemmas: Soundness follows by induction on derivations; completeness uses Henkin constructions.
repair_templates: Separate the soundness direction from the completeness direction.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: First-order compactness theorem
statement: If every finite subset of a first-order theory has a model, then the entire theory has a model.
conditions: The language and theory may be infinite.
typical_uses: Construct nonstandard models and prove existence by finite approximations.
common_misuses: Assuming the resulting model is finite or standard.
bridge_lemmas: Completeness plus finite proof uses only finitely many premises.
repair_templates: Verify model existence for each finite subtheory.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Downward and upward Loewenheim-Skolem pattern
statement: For suitable first-order theories, interpretations can be transferred to models of controlled infinite cardinalities using elementary substructures or compactness.
conditions: The language cardinality and desired infinite cardinal are specified.
conclusion: First-order theories cannot generally pin down an infinite cardinality up to isomorphism.
typical_uses: Diagnose claims of categoricity in first-order languages.
repair_templates: State whether the conclusion is elementary substructure, embedding, or isomorphism.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Godel incompleteness pattern
statement: A consistent effectively axiomatized theory capable of representing elementary arithmetic has a sentence independent of the theory; if sound, the sentence is true but unprovable.
conditions: The theory is recursively axiomatized, consistent, and sufficiently expressive for arithmetic coding.
conclusion: The theory is incomplete and cannot prove its own consistency under standard hypotheses.
typical_uses: Check purported complete effective axiomatizations of arithmetic.
common_misuses: Applying the theorem to finite or non-effective theories.
repair_templates: Verify effectiveness, consistency, and arithmetic representability.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Partial recursive function closure
statement: The partial recursive functions are generated from initial functions by composition, primitive recursion, and minimization, allowing divergence under unbounded search.
conditions: Functions are defined on natural numbers, possibly partially.
conclusion: The class is closed under the listed effective constructions.
common_misuses: Treating unbounded minimization as total without a witness.
repair_templates: State whether the minimization search is guaranteed to terminate.

source: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Full second-order semantics
statement: Second-order quantifiers range over all subsets or relations of the domain, not merely definable ones.
conditions: A second-order language and a nonempty structure are fixed.
conclusion: Second-order truth depends on the full power-set interpretation.
typical_uses: Distinguish full semantics from Henkin semantics.
common_misuses: Applying first-order compactness or completeness to full second-order logic.
bridge_lemmas: Second-order variables are assigned relations of the appropriate arity.
repair_templates: State explicitly whether semantics are full or Henkin.
